question: How does the guide characterize the nautical Navigation Rules?
choice_a: As voluntary guidelines with no legal force
choice_b: As recommendations that apply only on Lake Erie
choice_c: As the traffic laws of the waterways, legally binding for boat operators
choice_d: As rules that apply only to commercial vessels
explanation: The nautical rules are the traffic laws of the waterways and are legally binding for boat operators.

question: Under the Navigation Rules' definitions, what does "underway" mean?
choice_a: A vessel is traveling faster than idle speed
choice_b: A vessel has its engine running, regardless of motion
choice_c: A vessel is displaying navigation lights
choice_d: A vessel is not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground
explanation: "Underway" means that a vessel is not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground.

question: What is a "vessel not under command," per the Navigation Rules' definitions?
choice_a: A vessel which, through some exceptional circumstance, is unable to maneuver or keep out of the way of another vessel
choice_b: A vessel with no licensed operator aboard
choice_c: A vessel that has been reported stolen
choice_d: A sailing vessel with its sails down
explanation: A "vessel not under command" is one which, through some exceptional circumstance, is unable to maneuver or to keep out of the way of another vessel.

question: How must every vessel maintain a proper look-out, per the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: By sight only
choice_b: By sight and hearing, and all available means appropriate to the circumstances
choice_c: By radar only, if equipped
choice_d: Look-out is only required while operating in a channel
explanation: Every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means appropriate to the circumstances, to fully appraise the situation and risk of collision.

question: Which of the following is a factor a vessel must take into account when determining a safe speed?
choice_a: The vessel's registration number
choice_b: The number of years the operator has held a driver's license
choice_c: Visibility, traffic density, and maneuverability including stopping distance
choice_d: Whether the vessel is titled or merely registered
explanation: Safe speed factors include visibility, traffic density, maneuverability (stopping distance and turning ability), background light at night, wind/sea/current/hazard proximity, and draft in relation to water depth.

question: If a vessel operator is in doubt about whether a risk of collision exists, what should they assume?
choice_a: That no risk exists unless another vessel signals otherwise
choice_b: The question only matters in a narrow channel
choice_c: They should ask the other vessel by radio before assuming anything
choice_d: That risk of collision does exist
explanation: Every vessel shall use all available means to determine if risk of collision exists; if in doubt, such risk shall exist.

question: What quality must any action taken to avoid a collision have, per the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: It must be positive, made in ample time, and with due regard to good seamanship
choice_b: It must be a minor, barely noticeable course change
choice_c: It must always involve stopping the engine entirely
choice_d: It must be communicated in advance by VHF radio
explanation: Any action taken to avoid collision shall be positive and made in ample time, with due regard to good seamanship, and substantial enough to be readily apparent to another vessel.

question: In a narrow channel, a power vessel proceeding down bound with a following current has right-of-way over which vessel?
choice_a: A sailing vessel only
choice_b: An upbound vessel
choice_c: No other vessel -- down bound vessels always yield
choice_d: Any vessel engaged in fishing
explanation: In a narrow channel, a power vessel proceeding down bound with a following current shall have right-of-way over an upbound vessel.

question: In a narrow channel, which vessels must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel?
choice_a: Only vessels over 20 meters long
choice_b: Only sailing vessels
choice_c: Vessels less than 20 meters long, sailing vessels, fishing vessels, or vessels crossing the channel
choice_d: No vessel is ever required to give way in a narrow channel
explanation: Vessels less than 20 meters long, sailing vessels, vessels engaged in fishing, or vessels crossing the channel shall not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within a channel.

question: A vessel leaving a dock, slip, tie-up or mooring must do what regarding approaching vessels?
choice_a: Sound five short blasts and proceed
choice_b: Has the right-of-way over all approaching vessels
choice_c: Wait exactly 60 seconds before departing
choice_d: Yield the right-of-way to all vessels approaching
explanation: Vessels leaving a dock, slip, tie-up or mooring shall yield the right-of-way to all vessels approaching.

question: Two sailing vessels are approaching one another with the wind on different sides. Which vessel must keep out of the way of the other?
choice_a: The vessel which has the wind on its port side
choice_b: The vessel which has the wind on its starboard side
choice_c: Neither -- both must alter course equally
choice_d: Whichever vessel is smaller
explanation: When two sailing vessels approach with the wind on different sides, the vessel which has the wind on the port side shall keep out of the way of the other.

question: Two sailing vessels have the wind on the SAME side. Which vessel must keep out of the way?
choice_a: The leeward (downwind) vessel
choice_b: The windward (upwind) vessel
choice_c: Whichever vessel is under sail alone, without an engine
choice_d: Neither vessel needs to give way
explanation: When both sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the vessel which is to windward shall keep out of the way of the vessel which is to leeward.

question: Which vessel must keep out of the way in an overtaking situation?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken
choice_b: Whichever vessel is larger
choice_c: The vessel doing the overtaking
choice_d: Neither vessel needs to give way during overtaking
explanation: Any vessel overtaking another shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken.

question: In a head-on situation between two power-driven vessels, what is each vessel required to do, unless otherwise agreed?
choice_a: Alter course to port and pass on the starboard side of the other
choice_b: Stop engines and wait for the other vessel to pass
choice_c: Maintain course and speed without altering anything
choice_d: Alter course to starboard and pass on the port side of the other
explanation: When two power-driven vessels approach head-on, each shall alter course to starboard and pass on the port side of the other.

question: At night, when does a head-on situation exist between two power-driven vessels?
choice_a: When both red and green sidelights are visible
choice_b: When only a white masthead light is visible
choice_c: When only a stern light is visible
choice_d: Head-on situations cannot be determined at night
explanation: A head-on situation exists at night if both red and green sidelights are visible.

question: What does one short blast ("toot") of a horn signal to another vessel?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_b: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_c: Engine in reverse
choice_d: Danger
explanation: One short blast (toot) means "I intend to leave you on my port side."

question: What does two short blasts of a horn signal to another vessel?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_b: Coming out of a slip
choice_c: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_d: I am not under command
explanation: Two short blasts mean "I intend to leave you on my starboard side."

question: How many short blasts signal "danger" to another vessel?
choice_a: Two
choice_b: Three
choice_c: Four
choice_d: Five
explanation: Five short blasts (toot toot toot toot toot) signal danger.

question: What does a single prolonged blast (4-6 seconds) signal?
choice_a: Coming out of a slip
choice_b: Danger
choice_c: Engine in reverse
choice_d: I intend to leave you on my port side
explanation: A prolonged blast (4-6 seconds) signals that a vessel is coming out of a slip.

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels where risk of collision exists, which vessel must keep out of the way?
choice_a: The vessel which has the other on its port side
choice_b: The vessel which has the other on its starboard side
choice_c: Whichever vessel is traveling faster
choice_d: Neither vessel needs to give way in a crossing situation
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing and risk of collision exists, the vessel which has the other on its starboard side shall keep out of the way and avoid crossing ahead.

question: A vessel crossing a river must keep out of the way of what?
choice_a: Only sailing vessels on the river
choice_b: Nothing -- crossing vessels always have the right-of-way
choice_c: A power-driven vessel ascending or descending the river
choice_d: Only vessels moving faster than idle speed
explanation: A vessel crossing a river shall keep out of the way of a power-driven vessel ascending or descending the river.

question: What must a give-way vessel do, per the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Maintain its current course and speed at all times
choice_b: Sound its horn continuously until the other vessel responds
choice_c: Immediately stop its engine
choice_d: So far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear
explanation: Every vessel directed to keep out of the way of another shall, so far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear.

question: Under normal circumstances, what must a stand-on vessel do?
choice_a: Keep its course and speed
choice_b: Immediately alter course to starboard
choice_c: Stop engines and wait
choice_d: Sound five short blasts
explanation: Where one of two vessels is to keep out of the way, the other (the stand-on vessel) shall keep its course and speed.

question: A power-driven vessel taking action to avoid collision with another power vessel shall NOT do what?
choice_a: Reduce its speed
choice_b: Alter course to port for a vessel on its own port side
choice_c: Sound a horn signal
choice_d: Alter course to starboard
explanation: A power-driven vessel which takes action to avoid collision with another power vessel shall not alter course to port for a vessel on its own port side.

question: Under the responsibilities between vessels, a power vessel underway must keep out of the way of which of the following?
choice_a: A stand-on vessel in an overtaking situation
choice_b: Another power vessel in open water with no crossing risk
choice_c: A sailing vessel
choice_d: A vessel that is anchored outside a channel
explanation: A power vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in commercial fishing, and a sailing vessel.

question: A sailing vessel underway must keep out of the way of which vessel?
choice_a: A power-driven vessel with no special status
choice_b: A personal watercraft
choice_c: A vessel anchored in open water
choice_d: A vessel engaged in commercial fishing
explanation: A sailing vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in commercial fishing.

question: On a boat less than 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length, how far must the white masthead light and stern light be visible?
choice_a: 2 miles
choice_b: 1 mile
choice_c: 3 miles
choice_d: 5 miles
explanation: On boats less than 12 meters in length, the white masthead light and stern light must be visible for 2 miles.

question: On a boat less than 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length, how far must the red and green sidelights be visible?
choice_a: 1/2 mile
choice_b: 1 mile
choice_c: 2 miles
choice_d: 3 miles
explanation: On boats less than 12 meters in length, the red and green sidelights must be visible for 1 mile.

question: For power-driven vessels, which color light is displayed on the starboard side?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: White
choice_c: Green
choice_d: Yellow
explanation: For power vessels, a green light is displayed on the starboard side and a red light on the port side.

question: What color is an anchor light?
choice_a: A red light visible only from astern
choice_b: A green light visible from the bow
choice_c: A flashing yellow light
choice_d: An all-around white light
explanation: An anchor light is an all-around white light.

question: A sailing vessel less than 7 meters (23 feet) that cannot practically display the standard sailing vessel lights must instead show what?
choice_a: An electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light in sufficient time to prevent collision
choice_b: No light is required for vessels this small
choice_c: A flashing red beacon
choice_d: Two white lights, one forward and one aft
explanation: Sailing vessels less than 7 meters that cannot practically display the standard lights shall have an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light in sufficient time to prevent collision.

question: A vessel under oars that does not exhibit sailing-vessel lights must instead have what?
choice_a: No light is required for vessels under oars
choice_b: An electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light in sufficient time to prevent collision
choice_c: A red stern light only
choice_d: A green bow light only
explanation: A vessel under oars may exhibit sailing vessel lights, but if not, shall have an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light in sufficient time to prevent collision.

question: Which vessels are required to exhibit a white all-around anchor light while at anchor, per the guide?
choice_a: Only powercraft over 26 feet
choice_b: Only vessels operating on Lake Erie
choice_c: All vessels, including canoes and kayaks (with a narrow exception for small vessels away from channels)
choice_d: Only vessels anchored overnight for more than 8 hours
explanation: A white light visible all around the horizon shall be exhibited by all vessels, including canoes and kayaks, while at anchor -- except anchored vessels less than 7 meters not in or near a narrow channel, fairway, or where other vessels navigate.

question: When must a vessel display running lights or an anchor light, per the guide?
choice_a: Only during fog or heavy rain
choice_b: Only when operating on Lake Erie
choice_c: Only when carrying passengers for hire
choice_d: While underway, or at anchor between sunset and sunrise
explanation: All vessels are required to display running lights while underway or an anchor light if at anchor between sunset and sunrise.
